newsitem.title: CHINA: HK gov't moves on illegal children, colonial laws.
newsitem.headline: HK gov't moves on illegal children, colonial laws.

text.p: Hong Kong's new government, in power for just one week, will introduce draft bills on Wednesday to suspend laws passed in the twilight of British colonial rule and to allow deportation of children smuggled in illegally.
Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa's government also said on Tuesday it would accept proportional representation for 20 out of 60 legislature seats in elections planned for next year.
Under the system announced on Tuesday, pro-democracy parties are unlikely to repeat their strong showing of 1995 when they won the largest bloc of seats in the now-dissolved colonial assembly.
Led by lawyer Martin Lee, the pro-democracy parties have refused to join the Beijing-appointed legislature which took over after China regained Hong Kong on July 1.
Lee will lead former lawmakers in a protest rally outside the new legislature as it holds its first regular session on Wednesday.
Tung has hinted in recent days that a number of colonial-era laws would be suspended or repealed by the new legislature.

On Tuesday a government spokesman said seven laws, mostly covering workers' rights, should be suspended to "allow a proper and thorough scrutiny of the implications...to determine whether the provisions are in the public interest".
Tung's government will also introduce a bill to permit the deportation of children smuggled into Hong Kong from mainland China as the return to Beijing-rule neared.
Hundreds of children have crossed into Hong Kong in recent weeks to claim the right of abode and China says 60,000 more are waiting in neighbouring Guangdong province hoping to get in.
Secretary of Security Peter Lai, outlining the immigration bill, asked the legislature to rush it through on Wednesday to set up a "certificate of eligibility" system and stop a further influx.
"Any delay would be exploited by snakeheads (smugglers) who would spread rumours of an amnesty and there would be the possibility of hordes of children being smuggled in," Lai said.
Both bills must go through three readings in the 60-member provisional chamber before being adopted. The government said it hoped this could be done in a single day.
The new legislature replaced an elected colonial assembly, dissolved when Hong Kong reverted to Communist China on July 1 after 156 years of colonial rule.

Tung was visibly angry at a recent news conference over the question of the hastily passed laws. For many it came as no surprise that the new government's first order of business should be their suspension.
"It's quite disturbing," said law professor Raymond Wacks of the University of Hong Kong. "These laws were passed by an elected legislature."
But he said few had had any illusions that laws passed by the outgoing colonial assembly would remain long on the books.
"It would have been a surprise if this hadn't happened," he said.
